processing: A roasted or pan-finished bud-and-leaf green tea with no oxidation. The older Xueya form is tightly twisted and slightly hooked, while the modern Pingshui Rizhu brand favours a bud-like shape.
harvest_season: Spring, as with other Zhejiang greens; early, tender picking is the prized part.
appearance_dry: Older Rizhu Xueya is described as fine, slightly hooked and dark glossy green with frosty down; the modern form is shaped like a flower bud.
taste_profile: Modern tea is known for chestnut aroma and a fresh, mellow mouth with a sweet return.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for a Zhejiang green. One old description praises its staying power over five steeps, so do not stop after the first.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring green, today mostly under the Pingshui Rizhu regional brand, and best drunk within the year. Other names such as Rizhu Xueya still circulate. Pre-Qingming lots generally command more.
description:
Rizhu is the old-name tea of Shaoxing, from Rizhu Ridge on the northern side of the Kuaiji Mountains. Today you will mostly see it as Pingshui Rizhu, a regional brand that revives a name far older than the current product.

The tea has more than one look. Older descriptions of Rizhu Xueya, snow bud, have fine hooked strips compared to an eagle's claw, with a frost of down that explains the name. Modern promotion stresses a bud-like shape instead.

The modern selling line is simple: bud shape, chestnut aroma, fresh taste. The liquor is a bright tender green and the sweetness returns late, so try several steeps.

Do not assume today's tea tastes like what Song writers drank. Their tea was made in other ways, and the name is a link to a place more than a recipe. Buy for freshness and a clear Shaoxing origin.
history:
The ridge's tea is praised in Song writing. The line that among the teas of the two Zhe regions Rizhu ranks first is attributed to Ouyang Xiu.

Later accounts call it a tribute tea from the Song through the Qing, and one tells of a tribute garden reserved for the Kangxi emperor. These come from local and promotional writing, as does the story that Lu Xun liked it, so hold them loosely. The same writing says the tea nearly vanished before 1949.

Its modern revival is clearer: in 2011 Keqiao district adopted Pingshui Rizhu as its regional public brand.
